sentences.text: The genus Halszkaraptor contains only one known species, Halszkaraptor escuilliei.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — represents a subadult individual that was about one year old.
This young animal had a head about 7 cm long, a neck 20 cm long, a back 13 cm long, and a sacrum 5 cm long.
Halszkaraptor was about 60 centimeters long, roughly the size of a mallard duck.
The snout is transversely expanded at the front, creating a spoon-shaped profile when viewed from above.
The descending ramus of the postorbital bone in Halszkaraptor has a rod-like shape.
Halszkaraptor's neck vertebrae had extremely reduced neural spines, appearing as low crests on the second to fifth vertebrae and being completely absent on posterior cervical vertebrae.
On the second to fifth cervical vertebrae, the postzygapophyses, which normally occur in pairs, fused into a single lobe-shaped process.
The chevrons at the base of Halszkaraptor's tail were large and had a pentagonal profile.
The first phalanx of the third finger in Halszkaraptor's hand was 47% the length of the third metacarpal.
Halszkaraptor was named and described in 2017 by a team of researchers including Andrea Cau, Pascal Godefroit, and Rinchen Barsbold.
The holotype was found in an orange sandstone layer of the Bayn Dzak Member of the Djadochta Formation, dating to the late Campanian.
The holotype fossil dates to the late Campanian, approximately seventy-five million years ago.
The fossil was eventually returned to Mongolian authorities after being held by collectors and dealers.
The holotype displays evidence of a semiaquatic lifestyle, though some researchers question this ecology.
Neurovascular channels in the premaxilla probably housed electro-sensory organs.
Scientists used synchrotron scanning on the fossil to find evidence of a semi-aquatic lifestyle in the bones.
Halszkaraptor possessed adaptations for both terrestrial and aquatic life, including strong hind legs for running and paddle-like forelimbs for swimming.
Its short tail likely shifted the center of gravity forward, an adaptation more useful for swimming than walking.
Scientists believe Halszkaraptor hunted aquatic prey based on its sharp backward-curving teeth, long neck, and potential for detecting water vibrations via snout sensors.
Halszkaraptor was classified within the family Dromaeosauridae in 2017.
A new subfamily named Halszkaraptorinae was created to include Halszkaraptor and its relatives Hulsanpes and Mahakala.
Phylogenetic analysis determined that Halszkaraptorinae represents the most basal known group of dromaeosaurids.
Halszkaraptor lived during the Late Cretaceous period.
Halszkaraptor lived approximately 75 to 71 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
It is debated whether Halszkaraptor had a semiaquatic ecology.
It is notable that Halszkaraptor is one of only two known non-avian dinosaurs adapted to a semi-aquatic lifestyle, alongside spinosaurids and Natovenator.
